Article Title: US says Europe refused to join push for tariffs on India, China over Russian oil
Article Text:
File photo: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent

US defends 60-day pause on sanctions legislation

Bessent accuses Europe of financing Russia's war effort

Rubio calls India an important ally

Bessent questioned over whether Ukraine is a US ally

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent has accused European countries of refusing Washington's request to impose secondary tariffs on India and China for purchasing Russian oil, questioning why the United States should bear the burden of pressuring Moscow alone.Speaking to NBC News' Meet the Press on Sunday, Bessent said the Trump administration had approached European allies in the spring to seek coordinated action against countries buying Russian energy.“So we have asked—in the spring, I asked our European allies to join us in putting secondary tariffs on China, on India. They refused. So why should the US bear the burden?” Bessent said.He added that Washington could re-engage with its European partners, reiterating that President Donald Trump wanted to end the Russia-Ukraine war.“President Trump has made it clear he wants the killing to stop. And the so-called Graham bill gives the president the flexibility, gives him 60 days to assess the situation,” Bessent said.Bessent's remarks came after Trump temporarily waived certain provisions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, giving his administration 60 days to assess the potential consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs.Defending the decision, Bessent insisted that the administration had not lifted sanctions on Russia.“No sanctions were lifted on Friday,” he told NBC's Meet the Press, referring to Trump's executive order granting the waiver.The legislation, which received strong bipartisan support in Congress, provides for tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported into the United States from countries that are among the largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas, including India and China.Bessent said the pause would allow the administration to evaluate the situation before deciding on further measures. He also defended Trump's record on Russia, citing sanctions imposed on Russian energy companies Rosneft and Lukoil.“President Trump sanctioned the two largest Russian energy companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, which dealt a catastrophic blow to the Russian energy industry,” he said. “So no one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump.”US secretary of state Marco Rubio also defended the pause, saying the administration needed time to assess the consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs on the global and American economies.“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy, and even to the US economy,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday.Rubio said the administration was also considering pressures on global energy supplies arising from the Iran war, attacks by Houthi militants in Saudi Arabia and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine.Bessent also criticised European countries for continuing to purchase Russian oil and gas while supporting Ukraine.Citing shipments from Russia's Yamal facility, he said 140 cargoes had left during the first six months of the year, with 136 going to European countries, including Belgium, Spain, France and the Netherlands.Those shipments were worth more than $8 billion, he said.“The Europeans have given Russia and Vladimir Putin more money than they've given the Ukrainians. They continue to gorge on Russian energy,” Bessent said.He added that the United States imported $4 billion worth of Russian products, including $1.8 billion in fertilisers, while European countries imported more than 10 times as much.Bessent also pointed to the UK's decision in May to waive its embargo on diesel and jet fuel made using Russian crude, questioning why similar criticism had not been directed at other countries.Rubio said Washington needed to consider the energy requirements of countries such as India before deciding whether to impose tariffs or sanctions.“These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others,” Rubio said.He added that countries such as India had diversified their energy supplies but could not immediately stop importing Russian energy.The comments came amid criticism of Trump's decision to pause enforcement of the sanctions legislation. Indian-American lawmakers Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam criticised the move, arguing that it weakened pressure on Russia and undermined Congress' authority.During the same NBC programme, Bessent was asked three times whether the United States considered Ukraine an ally. He did not give a direct yes-or-no answer.“We provide the three different things ... to Ukraine, so that’s what you do for an ally. We’re not providing those to Russia,” he said on the second occasion.Bessent said Washington supported Ukraine by providing intelligence, Starlink support and allowing Nato countries to purchase American weapons for transfer to Kyiv.He also questioned why European members of Nato had not supplied Ukraine with more Patriot missile systems, arguing that they had the capability to do so.His comments followed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's appearance on the programme, during which he warned that it would be a “historic mistake” for the United States to side with Russia.“We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions because I think that it's all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help the United States,” Zelensky said of Trump.Bessent criticised the Ukrainian president for publicly accusing Washington and Elon Musk of restricting resources used by Ukrainian forces. He called the allegations “very reckless”, according to NBC News.Bessent maintained that Trump wanted to end the war through a negotiated settlement, saying the conflict had to stop and that the president was working towards that outcome.
Article Summary: US treasury secretary Scott Bessent accused European countries of refusing Washington's request to impose secondary tariffs on India and China for purchasing Russian oil. He questioned why the U.S. should bear the burden of pressuring Moscow alone. Comments came after Trump temporarily waived certain provisions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.

Article Title: Oil prices ease as Trump waives Russia sanctions, Middle East risks persist
Article Text:
Crude prices ease below $110 per barrel

Oil prices fell on Monday as US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia raised the prospect of additional fuel supplies entering the market. However, continuing security threats in the Middle East and uncertainty over US-Iran negotiations kept the outlook for crude volatile.Brent crude declined $1.56, or 1.42%, to $108.3, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was down 0.25, or 0.25%, at $101.2 a barrel.The previous week, US President Donald Trump had signed an executive order granting a waiver on key sanctions and tariffs imposed under the law known as the Graham Act. The legislation was signed last month after lawmakers urged the president to put pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.Secretary of state Marco Rubio said Trump would use up to 60 days to evaluate the economic consequences of the waiver.The move came after Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to export diesel to the US. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the US actions, saying they would hurt Ukraine.Brent crude had climbed to $110 a barrel briefly on Friday, marking its first such level since May, as mounting tensions in the Middle East heightened concerns about the security of shipping routes and the availability of global energy supplies.The pressure on supplies has been compounded by attacks on commercial vessels. Gulf crude flows fell to approximately 8.5 million barrels per day on a seven-day average last week, down from more than 20 million barrels per day in the previous week, according to analytics firm Kpler. In a note issued on Friday, the firm also reported at least 10 confirmed incidents involving commercial vessels during the week.The risk of a wider regional confrontation remained in focus, with Egypt stating that it was prepared to offer Saudi Arabia the support required to protect its security and stability against Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.Despite Monday’s decline, crude markets face another week of potential price swings. Supply concerns across West Asia and stalled negotiations between the US and Iran are fuelling fears of further disruptions, while measures aimed at easing shortages are providing some relief, analysts said.Market participants will look to upcoming inventory figures for a clearer picture of supply and demand. The data under scrutiny include weekly crude stock estimates from the American Petroleum Institute (API), inventories at Cushing, total US oil stocks and crude imports.Developments around the Strait of Hormuz will also remain crucial to the market outlook. Any interruption to shipments through the strategic waterway could further restrict global oil supplies, adding to the uncertainty surrounding prices.
Article Summary: Brent crude declined $1.56, or 1.42%, to $108.3 a barrel on Monday. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was down 0.25, or 0. 25%, at $101.2 a barrel. US President Donald Trump had signed an executive order granting a waiver on key sanctions and tariffs imposed under the Graham Act.

Article Title: Rupee rises to 94.80 against US dollar, but crude oil threatens recovery
Article Text:
Rupee strengthens against US dollar

NEW DELHI: Rupee began the week on a cheerful note, inching towards the 94 mark against US dollar on Monday. The currency strengthened by 9 paise to 94.80 against the greenback in early trade, extending its recovery for a third consecutive session. This followed Friday's close of 94.89, when the currency had gained 10 paise.The Reserve Bank of India 's structural forex interventions continued to support rupee, although elevated crude oil prices remain a key risk to sustaining the gains.Forex traders said that the currency has staged its sharpest rally in seven months, but sustained pressure from expensive crude, rising US treasury yields and continued foreign capital outflows has kept the currency under strain. The RBI has stepped up its market interventions amid these pressures.CR forex advisors MD Amit Pabari said the currency's movement below 95 over the past three sessions has brought the 94.80–94.70 range into focus."With USDINR holding below 95.00 for the last 3 sessions, the focus shifts to 94.80–94.70. A sustained break below 94.80 could open the way towards 94.00 over the coming weeks."However, elevated crude prices remain a key risk, and the rupee's next move will depend on whether oil eases or sustains its surge," he added.Brent crude, which had surged to $110 per barrel, was trading at $107.79 per barrel in futures trade, down 1.88%. Attacks on commercial vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, interruptions to oil flows and threats to Saudi energy infrastructure have fuelled concerns about a prolonged supply shock.The dollar index, which tracks the US currency against a basket of six currencies, stood at 101.83, marginally lower by 0.01%.Meanwhile, domestic equities came under pressure in early trade. The BSE Sensex shed 470.50 points to reach 74,318, while NSE Nifty50 declined 147.10 points to 22,999.05.Foreign investors, however, returned as net buyers of Indian equities on Friday. Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) purchased shares worth Rs 1,165.92 crore on a net basis, according to exchange data.The country's forex reserves also registered another weekly decline. Reserve Bank of India data released on Friday showed that reserves fell by USD 8.578 billion to USD 726.027 billion in the week ended October 9.The fall followed a $12.952 billion decline in the preceding reporting week, which had brought India's foreign exchange reserves down to $734.606 billion.
Article Summary: Rupee inching towards 94 mark against US dollar on Monday. Currency strengthened by 9 paise to 94.80 against the greenback in early trade. This followed Friday's close of 94.89, when the currency had gained 10 paise.

Article Title: Renting a house in UP? Proposed Rs 1,000 stamp duty on Rs 2 lakh annual rent aims to cut costs, boost registered rent agreements and protect tenants and landlords, here’s how
Article Text:
One drawback of verbal or unregistered rental arrangements is the difficulty of establishing proof. (Image for representative purpose only)

What is the current trend?

How could the proposed UP rent law benefit tenants and landlords?

Recently, the Uttar Pradesh government announced plans to revamp the state's tenancy rules, including changes to the stamp duty and registration charges that are applicable to rental agreements.At a press conference, Ravindra Jaiswal, Minister of State for Stamp and Registration Fees, said the state government was considering a stamp duty of Rs 1,000 on rent agreements where the annual rent amounts to Rs 2 lakh.Under Indian law, residential rent agreements covering a period of 11 months do not require compulsory registration, according to an ET report. This is one reason why 11-month agreements are so common.One drawback of verbal or unregistered rental arrangements is the difficulty of establishing proof. Such agreements generally cannot be relied upon as evidence unless a court permits their use.Circle rates are another factor behind the widespread practice of keeping residential tenancy agreements unregistered.Also Read | Homebuyers paid Rs 2.06 crore but got no flat, builder said payments meant accepting delay; Bombay HC orders interest payout from 2017 saying RERA allows for unconditional right to monthly interest The proposed changes could offer practical advantages to both tenants and property owners, particularly by making it easier and less expensive to register rental agreements.Legal experts expect the proposed changes to complement the Uttar Pradesh Urban Premises Tenancy Regulation Act, 2021.Malav Virani, Partner at MDP Legal, told ETthat the government's primary concern was the low rate of registration of rent agreements across the state.Under the existing system, stamp duty and registration charges for tenancy agreements were calculated as a proportion of the rent, at roughly 4%, based on four times the property's circle rate.Virani explained that this formula could result in a substantial stamp duty burden even when the rent agreed upon was relatively modest.To avoid these expenses, many landlords and tenants opted for verbal arrangements rather than entering into written agreements. Even when they prepared written documents, they often left them unregistered.Also Read | She bought shares for Rs 13.5 lakh and sold them for Rs 77.47 lakh after 18 months; taxman denied capital gains exemption, but ITAT gives relief and deletes Rs 79 lakh in additions According to Virani, the reforms are intended to make the Act easier to implement by addressing the cost of registering tenancy agreements, which has discouraged people from doing so. Another objective is to reduce landlord-tenant disputes reaching the courts because the parties lack properly documented agreements or rely on informal arrangements.Virani said the lower stamp duty and registration costs would provide relief to tenants and encourage them to formalise their rental arrangements. Registering an agreement would also help tenants secure the protections available under the Act.Virani says: “Armed with a registered agreement, tenants will enjoy a strong legal standing with proof of tenure, agreed rent, and other terms being documented.” Such records could prove important if a landlord tries to evict a tenant unlawfully, challenges the agreed rent or denies that a tenancy arrangement exists.Having a properly registered agreement is intended to strengthen the legal position of both parties and discourage practices that violate their contractual rights.Landlords, too, stand to benefit because the terms of the tenancy would be recorded in writing and formally registered.According to Virani, this documentation can help protect property owners if a tenant refuses to leave after the agreement expires, defaults on rent payments or commits similar breaches of the tenancy terms.Also Read | He bought a home, gave it for redevelopment years later and sold new flat for Rs 1.95 crore within 8 days; taxman denied LTCG exemption and added Rs 80.14 lakh, but ITAT grants relief
Article Summary: The Uttar Pradesh government announced plans to revamp the state's tenancy rules. The proposed changes could offer practical advantages to both tenants and property owners. Legal experts expect the proposed changes to complement the Uttar Pradesh Urban Premises Tenancy Regulation Act, 2021.

Article Title: 'Geography is real': Rubio says India-US trade deal close, explains Trump admin's stance on Russian oil
Article Text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio

Why the US is taking another look at Russian oil sanctions

Graham bill and geopolitics

NEW DELHI: US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Monday said that India and the US are close to finalising a trade deal. He also explained the reason behind Washington's consideration of India energy needs before imposing sanctions or tariffs linked to Russian oil.Speaking to reporters in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, Rubio said the US had waived some sanctions in recent months to limit their impact on global energy supplies and prices."We've had to waive sanctions over the past few months because of the impact on global supplies and prices...We have to manage all of these things.”Explaining how Washington was balancing trade negotiations with India and decisions on sanctions, Rubio said countries had to consider several factors when making foreign policy decisions, including how easily they could access alternative energy sources.“We're trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that. That's one of the things we taken into consideration when the President makes a decision about national security waivers and things of that nature. Every country has a complex set of factors that it has to take into account. Geography is real. For some countries, it's very difficult to acquire energy from alternative sources.That's not an excuse, but all of that has to be balanced when making foreign policy..."Rubio is currently in Uzbekistan and is scheduled to visit Mumbai on Tuesday to meet external affairs minister S Jaishankar. He will also travel to Jamnagar later in the week, which is home to one of the world's largest refineries.Rubio's remarks come after US President Donald Trump waived several sanctions related to Russian fuel sales that were due to take effect under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.The law, which has now been paused, would have allowed the US to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods imported from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil or natural gas. India and China are among these countries.Rubio said the proposed measures would affect not just Russia but also countries that buy its energy. The US wants to use a 60-day period to study how the sanctions and tariffs could affect the global economy and its own economy."These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," Rubio said.He said India had diversified its energy sources but still bought a significant amount of energy from Russia. Switching to other suppliers immediately was not easy, he added."You've got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it's hard to pivot from one day to the next. But they're also an important ally and partner of the United States. So we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is," he added.Rubio also said the US was considering changes in the global situation since the Graham bill was passed. He pointed to the growing conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia, along with the war between Russia and Ukraine.He said global energy supplies were under pressure because of several factors, including Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and damage to energy infrastructure during the Russia-Ukraine war."I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this, given all the different things that are that are going on in the world right now, including the pressure on global energy supplies that are happening not just because of Iran and not just because of the Straits of Hormuz, but increasingly because of the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia, and because of the war with Ukraine and Russia, where energy infrastructure is being hit, and so that's having an impact on global prices as well," he said.Meanwhile, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal last week said that the first part of the agreement had been finalised and had moved to the legal drafting stage. "US bilateral trade agreement's first tranche has been finalised and it is going through final contours, the legal drafting and we hope to be able to finalise that soon and operationalise that once we get the competitive advantage over our peer countries," Goyal said.
Article Summary: US secretary of state Marco Rubio says India and the US are close to finalising a trade deal. He also explained the reason behind Washington's consideration of India energy needs before imposing sanctions or tariffs linked to Russian oil. Rubio is currently in Uzbekistan and is scheduled to visit Mumbai on Tuesday.

As times have gone by, there has been a change in the commercial face of the Delhi-NCR region, wherein existing retail zones in Delhi have been replaced by new business and consumer zones in Gurugram. The four-decade journey of SMARR Realty has evolved within this changing scenario. With more than 3.5 million sq. ft.of developed space, two hotels, nine malls and a portfolio of over 350 national and international retail brands, the company’s presence reflects the changing scale and character of the region’s growth.Its journey has been shaped not just by expansion, but by an understanding of what different locations need as their surrounding communities grow and change. SMARR Realty believes that the success of a project lies in how well it responds to the needs of its location. From retail and commercial spaces to hospitality, the company’s focus has been on understanding how businesses operate, how people use these spaces and what will keep them relevant over time. This thinking continues to shape SMARR’s approach to development and its plans for the region.said a spokesperson for SMARR Realty.Delhi, particularly Rohini, formed an important part of SMARR Realty’s presence in the region. Crown Heights, spread across approximately 2.75 lakh sq. ft., reflects this mix, accommodating retail brands, offices, a car showroom and a gym. Its proximity to Rithala Metro station, along with its connection to Crowne Plaza Rohini, adds to the range of uses within the development. The company’s portfolio also includes Vikas Surya Shopping Mall, with around 2 lakh sq. ft. of retail space across four floors, and Ring Road Mall, located along the Outer Ring Road. The City Centre Rohini is another project that covers about 4 lakhs square feet. These projects clearly show how extensive is the portfolio of SMARR Realty in Delhi on account of its location, format and commercial requirements.Besides, as Gurugram emerged as a major commercial centre within Delhi-NCR, SMARR Realty extended its presence into the city’s newer districts. In Sector 90, Sapphire Ninety covers approximately 5.5 lakh sq. ft. of built-up area, bringing together retail outlets, dining, fitness, gaming and a four-screen multiplex. Further along this growth corridor, SMARR Vista Square in Sector 82A offers around 4 lakh sq. ft. of gross leasable area, with brands such as SPAR, Shoppers Stop, BLAAZE and Eatree, alongside Devgn Cinex. The portfolio also includes Holiday Inn in Sector 90, with 259 rooms and suites, banquet facilities and access to adjoining retail and entertainment options. Together, these developments reflect the breadth of the company’s approach in Gurugram, where retail, hospitality and leisure have taken shape as complementary parts of its commercial presence.The next phase of SMARR Realty’s growth is taking shape in New Gurugram, where ongoing developments in Sectors 89 and 92 are set to add to the region’s expanding commercial infrastructure. The company’s projects include Vista Corner, Vista Centre and Vista Avenue in Sector 89, along with City Centre 92 in Sector 92. Planned across a mix of retail, restaurants, entertainment and office spaces, these developments are expected to cater to a wider range of business and consumer needs, with anchor stores adding to their commercial mix. Vista Avenue is also planned to feature a 252-key Le Méridien hotel, while City Centre 92 has a proposed 48,000 sq. ft. D-Mart hypermarket. Together, these projects mark the next stage of the company’s expansion across Delhi-NCR.Thus, from Delhi’s established retail centres to Gurugram’s newer commercial corridors, SMARR Realty’s four-decade journey reflects the changing nature of business and urban life across the region. Its portfolio spans retail, commercial and hospitality developments, with the next phase of growth taking shape in New Gurugram. As these districts continue to develop, the company’s story remains closely tied to the region’s own commercial evolution.
Article Summary: With more than 3.5 million sq. ft. of developed space, two hotels, nine malls and a portfolio of over 350 national and international retail brands, the company’s presence reflects the changing scale and character of the Delhi-NCR region. SMARR Realty believes that the success of a project lies in how well it responds to the needs of its location.

Article Title: Homebuyers paid Rs 2.06 crore but got no flat, builder said payments meant accepting delay; Bombay HC orders interest payout from 2017 saying RERA allows for unconditional right to monthly interest
Article Text:
The Bombay High Court examined whether accepting delayed performance could deprive homebuyers of their right to interest under Section 18 of RERA. (Image for representative purpose only)

What the case is about

Why did the court rule in favour of homebuyers?

Significance of ruling

What happens if the possession of your dream home is delayed? You buy an apartment, sign an agreement, make the necessary payments, but the builder repeatedly fails to deliver the flat on time. Are you entitled to interest payout under RERA Act?In one such case, the Bombay High Court has ordered the builder to pay interest and ruled that buyers have an unconditional right to monthly interest in case of project delays.Two homebuyers filed a case against the builder. The dispute concerned an apartment for which they had signed the sale agreement in 2014, with possession due by June 30, 2017.The flat's consideration was Rs 1.95 crore. By the time of the complaint, the buyers had paid Rs 2.06 crore, including the consideration paid to the promoter, stamp duty, registration charges and applicable taxes.Also Read | US-based daughter files case against parents seeking share in properties; Karnataka HC rejects her ‘ancestral’ claim, saying they were father's separate assets, not coparcenary property However, when they didn’t get the possession by the agreed deadline, the buyers approached MahaRERA, seeking possession along with interest for the delay. In January 2019, the authority directed the developer to hand over the apartment with an occupancy certificate by December 31, 2019, while allowing the buyers to seek interest at a later stage.The buyers appealed. In March 2021, the Maharashtra Real Estate Appellate Tribunal directed the promoter to pay interest at the State Bank of India's highest marginal cost of lending rate plus 2% on the amount paid, from July 1, 2017, until possession was handed over.It also awarded Rs 25,000 in costs.The builder challenged that order before the Bombay High Court. The developer's argument was that by continuing to pay installments under revised schedules, and by not objecting to its letters announcing new dates, the buyers had in effect accepted the delay.The promoter relied on Section 55 of the Indian Contract Act, which addresses the consequences of accepting delayed contractual performance without notifying the other party of an intention to claim compensation.The developer also invoked contractual force majeure provisions and the COVID-19 pandemic.Also Read | Grandmother and her son gifted 2.5-acre land to his second wife, who sold it; his daughter from first marriage claimed it was ancestral, but Madras HC rejects her plea According to Gaurav Dasgupta, Partner, Khaitan & Co, this is one of the most homebuyer-friendly rulings he has seen this year.Its message is simple: a developer cannot turn a buyer's patience into a waiver.The Bombay High Court examined whether accepting delayed performance could deprive homebuyers of their right to interest under Section 18 of RERA. It held that the statutory protection could not be made conditional on giving the notice contemplated under Section 55 of the Contract Act.The Bombay High Court rejected this since RERA is a special act for real estate, which overrides a general act like contract act, when there is a conflict between the provisions.“It held that Section 18 of RERA gives a buyer who stays with a delayed project an unconditional right to monthly interest. Following the Supreme Court, it said that right cannot be cut down by conditions or by events the buyer does not control. RERA is a beneficial legislation, and the court upheld the spirit of the act,” explains Gaurav Dasgupta.Also Read | Man enters JDA for land, gets 6 flats from builder and transfers 5 to wife, but gets tax notice; ITAT Delhi deletes Rs 4.14 crore additions after finding no stock-in-trade conversion or sale The developer's letters were information, not a renegotiation, according to the court.“A new date cannot be agreed informally by conduct, and in an ongoing RERA project the only lawful way to extend time is to extend the registration with the regulator after following due process of law. The Court also refused to let the developer rely on Covid-19, because the pandemic came long after the 2017 deadline had already passed,” Dasgupta tells TOI.In earlier similar cases, the court had given a ruling about payment of interest from the advent of RERA, but in this case, the court went on to uphold the allowing of interest from the date of original possession, even though it was before RERA came into force.The court dismissed the builder’s appeal which argued that the buyers had accepted changes to the possession schedule and could not subsequently claim interest without giving the developer notice. The High Court held that Section 18 of RERA protects a buyer's right to interest for delayed possession, even when the buyer chooses to remain in the project.Explaining the purpose of the legislation, the court said RERA was enacted “to protect the interest of consumer in the real estate sector”. It then clarified the right available to buyers who decide not to withdraw from a delayed project.The court held that Section 18 gives buyers an “unqualified absolute right” to accept delayed performance without giving up their claim to interest for every month of delay.Also Read | He bought a diesel SUV for Rs 13.69 lakh; but repeated DPF issues followed; consumer commission finds deficiency in service and awards Rs 10.99 lakh refund, 9% interest and compensation The promoter had argued that the buyers' conduct showed acceptance of revised possession dates. However, the High Court noted that the appellate tribunal had found “no authentic evidence” that they had accepted the revised possession date or waived their right to interest.The court also examined the developer's communications. It observed that these primarily informed buyers about the delay and offered assurances about completion. As the judgment states, “The revised timelines are couched in a manner so as to be in nature of information requiring no further acts by the allottees.”Importantly, the court held that even if the buyers had accepted the revised date, that would not extinguish their statutory entitlement. It stated: “Even accepting that there was acceptance of revised date of possession, considering Section 18 of RERA Act, the allottees were well within their rights to accept the delayed performance without foregoing their right to interest for delayed possession.”On the pandemic defence, the court noted that the contractual deadline was June 2017 and the project's revised completion date under RERA registration was December 2019. COVID-19 came later and, the court held, “does not impact the performance of the contract.”The Bombay High Court therefore upheld the direction to pay interest from July 1, 2017, until possession was handed over, and dismissed the promoter's second appeal on June 18, 2026.According to Gaurav Dasgupta, for homebuyers, paying installments on time while a project runs late does not cost you your interest claim.“Thus, it is important to keep faith in RERA and not violate any provisions of payment as agreed in the project timeline and then seek legal recourse for any violation on the part of the developer, including interest and costs,” he says.For developers, the lesson is just as clear.“If timelines slip, the answer is a formal extension under RERA, not reassuring letters to buyers. Interest liability starts on the contractual date and keeps running unless the extension is expressly agreed under the due process established under RERA – getting approval of 2/3of the allottees and approval of RERA,” he adds.It’s important to note that the ruling has been challenged before the Supreme Court through a special leave petition filed on 24 July 2026.The developer’s advocate had initially said that an out-of-court settlement was being explored, but later stated that they want full-fledged hearing in the appeal, says Dasgupta.The question the Supreme Court may now have to answer is whether this long-established Contract Act rule has any role left in RERA disputes.
Article Summary: The Bombay High Court has ruled that buyers have an unconditional right to monthly interest in case of project delays. The dispute concerned an apartment for which they had signed the sale agreement in 2014. The buyers had paid Rs 2.06 crore, including the consideration paid to the promoter, stamp duty, registration charges and applicable taxes.

Article Title: PNB ventures to win back young customers
Article Text:
The move is part of an exercise to win back customers who have flocked to more nimble private banks in recent years

NEW DELHI: From facilitating loans to startups to special savings accounts for students and credit card offers, state-run Punjab National Bank (PNB) is rolling out the red carpet for young customers.“Every young person wants to hold a credit card today, so our effort is to fulfil that. Second, we are easing the loan approval process for them, particularly for startups where they can avail credit digitally without getting involved in paperwork. We have also come up with a special savings scheme for them. Efforts are underway to get in touch with educational institutions, so that we can tap into the young age cohort,” PNB managing director and CEO Ashok Chandra told TOI.The move is part of an exercise to win back customers who have flocked to more nimble private banks in recent years, backed by better technology and a suite of products, often peddled by intrusive relationship managers. Recently, finance minister FM Nirmala Sitharaman had exhorted state-run banks to adopt a “lifecycle” approach and aim to become the preferred financial partner, from campus to career and beyond.Having reported a 13% rise in net profit to Rs 5,532 crore in the Sept quarter, Chandra is hopeful of the momentum sustaining with deposit and credit growth being on track in the current financial year, with no pressure to increase the deposit rates, at least for the time being.Besides, Chandra said El Nino had so far not impacted the bank’s loan book as it had seen sustained demand in its strongholds of north and north-western India, though he is keeping a close watch. “All sectors are behaving well. Growth is happening. Stress is at its lowest levels. As of now, there is no impact on our books... and we are watchful and mindful of it.”
Article Summary: The move is part of an exercise to win back customers who have flocked to more nimble private banks in recent years. Recently, finance minister FM Nirmala Sitharaman had exhorted state-run banks to adopt a ‘lifecycle’ approach and aim to become the preferred financial partner.

Article Title: Amid UPI user surge, Visa bets on affluent consumers
Article Text:
Competition in premium cards is also shifting beyond traditional benefits such as airport lounge access

MUMBAI: Visa, the world’s largest payments network, is expanding its focus in India towards affluent consumers, cross-border spending and higher-value payment services as UPI dominates everyday transactions such as groceries. The payment company is also expanding beyond interchange fees into B2B fund transfers, data consulting, cyber-resilience and AI-enabled threat detection.Visa group country manager Suresh Sethi said there is a segmentation in the digital payments market, where UPI is being used increasingly for day-to-day low-value payments while credit cards are used for other aspects of life. “We naturally also segment our markets. For us, what becomes very important is one, the entire affluent segment which is expanding as more people move from the mass-affluent segment into the affluent category,” said Sethi. The rise in overseas travel is creating another opportunity for card payments. “When you look at cross-border travel, Visa does bring the capability of global acceptance. You can virtually carry one single card with you when you’re travelling globally,” he said.Competition in premium cards is also shifting beyond traditional benefits such as airport lounge access. Foreign-exchange pricing and curated privileges are becoming more important, with zero-FX products allowing overseas transactions at the bank-rate conversion without a markup. Sethi said dynamic currency conversion has also encouraged consumers to use cards instead of prepaid forex instruments. Visa has expanded premium offerings including Infinite Privilege and Infinite Reserve.
Article Summary: Visa is expanding its focus in India towards affluent consumers, cross-border spending and higher-value payment services. The payment company is also expanding beyond interchange fees into B2B fund transfers, data consulting, cyber-resilience and AI-enabled threat detection.

Article Title: ‘We are learning to live with weaker currency’: Arvind Panagariya
Article Text:
Arvind Panagariya

TOI

Excerpts:

Sitting in New York, how do you see the

Indian economy

evolving? What is the feedback that you’re getting from colleagues and investors?

Given the headwinds due to west Asia in terms of higher cost, logistics, there is nervousness. Is that a big challenge?

A big concern with a weaker rupee has been that import bill rises.

India has signed multiple trade agreements

that reduce tariffs

bilaterally. What else needs to be done?

What about the bilateral investment treaty?

Do you see future

American presidents weaponising tariffs the way Trump has done?

Columbia University professor and 16th Finance Commission chairman Arvind Panagariya, who was in India for the Kautilya Conclave, spoke to, arguing that a weaker rupee will not just make exports competitive but will also keep the prices of finished imported goods higher. In an interview, he suggested tariff cuts, doing away with quality control orders and revisiting bilateral investment treaties.The general perception of the Indian economy is very positive. My assessment is that we will continue to grow at 7-8%. Manufacturinggrowth of 10% or so in the last three years gives me a lot of confidence; it is a very positive sign for the future. Inflation has remained stable, current account deficit has been very manageable. So, the vitals are all good.I don’t see our entrepreneurs nervous about growth prospects. Headwinds have been there and entrepreneurs have learnt to live with these things. We emerged very quickly and robustly from Covid. Our exports to the US and overall went up despite Trump’s tariffs, which shows that exporters have learnt to cope with this uncertainty.Finally, we seem to also be learning that currency depreciation is not always a bad thing. It is a very important change in our own attitudes. Indian products have to be competitive in the domestic market compared to imported goods.The increase in the cost of imports basically tells you that our goods are more competitive relative to the foreign goods. The cost of my inputs rises, but the cost of the goods that are coming in to compete with my (finished) goods rises even more. Our exports did so well between 2000 and 2011 because the dollar appreciated against the rupee between 1991 and 2002 by 170%. But it stayed around that level till 2011 or so, actually the rupee appreciated in nominal terms, before weakening. As a result, after crossing $300 billion in 2011-12, it fell below that mark and only increased post-Covid.This is much needed and I also want the agreement with the US to go through as it will not only give us access, it will also lead to the opening up of our own markets, which is very much required. Several QCOs have been suspended but there are many more that need to be repealed because they are offering protection. The Bureau of Indian Standards does not have the staff to implement them domestically and the intent seems to be protectionist. India is also among the top users of anti-dumping duty. Anti-dumping is sometimes even more pernicious than tariffs because these duties can be very large and also very targeted as you go after your cheapest supplier.We need to take a comprehensive look at the bilateral investment treaties because if we are going to attract foreign investors then we have to see what our competitors are doing, what China is doing, what Vietnam is doing.The US commitment to WTO has certainly weakened. The current President has acted as if WTO really doesn’t matter. The only restraint on him has been domestic US laws and even that he has at times neglected. I doubt if future presidents will do like that. But what has happened permanently, and is something that was already underway, is the weakening of the WTO discipline. Subsidies were given, like through the Chips Act during the Biden administration, which was in violation of WTO rules. With the appellate body not functioning there is no way it can be addressed.
Article Summary: The general perception of the Indian economy is very positive. My assessment is that we will continue to grow at 7-8%. Manufacturinggrowth of 10% or so in the last three years gives me a lot of confidence. Inflation has remained stable, current account deficit has been very manageable.

Article Title: Asian shares are mixed with tech stocks volatile, and oil falls on Trump's Russian sanctions waiver
Article Text:
Asian shares remain mixed

Asian shares were mixed Monday as volatility in technology stocks persisted, while U.S. equity futures edged higher ahead of another week of American corporate earnings results.Oil prices fell more than 2% after U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sweeping sanctions on Russia, including on Russian energy.A sell-off of technology shares from Asia to Wall Street recently put downward pressure on stock markets, as investor concerns grow over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom.South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index was up 1.8% to 5,768.01 on Monday, after falling sharply last week. The Kospi is down more than 17% over the past month, and still well below the 9,000 mark it crossed in June at its peak on the global AI frenzy.Samsung Electronics was up 1.2%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix added 0.4%.Japan’s Nikkei 225 lost 0.6% to 64,916.70. Japanese chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 2.6%, and OpenAI investor SoftBank Group dropped 2%.“We’ve been arguing for a while that volatility in tech stocks would pick up as the AI bubble continued to inflate: sharp and short-lived sell-offs were common as the ‘dotcom’ bubble inflated, for example, even as the market ultimately made very large gains on net,” Capital Economics Head of Markets for Asia Pacific Thomas Mathews wrote in a commentary Monday.Hong Kong’s stock market was closed because of a holiday. The Shanghai Composite index edged 0.4% higher to 3,730.92, after China reported better-than-expected growth of 4.5% for its economy in the July-September quarter.CXMT, China’s leading memory chipmaker, fell more than 7% despite the company forecasting a strong profit for the first nine months.Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was 0.4% higher at 8,845.70.Taiwan’s Taiex fell 0.6%. India’s Sensex slipped 0.9%.Indonesia’s benchmark stock index fell over 5% at its peak, to its lowest level since 2020, after it plunged over 11% on Friday following a warning from index provider MSCI that it would downgrade the country from its “emerging market” status.On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 declined 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.3%, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite sank 2.1%.Investors this week are watching for more big corporate earnings results from the U.S., including Meta, Netflix, General Motors, Tesla and IBM. Strong company earnings have been one factor that’s been keeping U.S. stocks robust lately.As technology shares face rising uncertainties, experts say government bonds might stand to benefit as investors look for relatively safe assets, though the bond market had also been turbulent over the past few weeks.The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury eased to around 5.07% early Monday, compared with roughly 5.13% Friday. It had hit 5.35% earlier this month at its highest level since 2002, as inflation worries from the Iran war-driven energy shock and growing U.S. government debt pushed yields higher — investors demanded more in return because of the additional risks.Oil prices were down early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, falling 2.5% to $107.16 per barrel.Benchmark U.S. crude dropped 2.2% to $96.84 per barrel.Oil fell after Trump late Friday signed an executive order to put new broad U.S. sanctions against Russia on hold just days before they were to come into effect, drawing disappointment from Ukraine, with the move likely resulting in more energy exports from Russia.Trump's decision came not long after he said earlier this month he had reached a diesel deal with Russia in an attempt to bring down elevated U.S. fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.But even with the decline, oil prices have remained elevated compared with those seen before the Iran war. Global oil supply risks are still high amid tensions in the Middle East, including uncertainty surrounding oil transport in the Strait of Hormuz, adding upward pressure to prices.The U.S. dollar fell to 157.98 Japanese yen from 158.10 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1218, down from $1.1234.
Article Summary: South Korea's benchmark Kospi index was up 1.8% to 5,768.01 on Monday, after falling sharply last week. China's Shanghai Composite index edged 0.4% higher to 3,730.92, after China reported better-than-expected growth of 4.5% for its economy in the July-September quarter. Oil prices fell more than 2% after U.S. President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sweeping sanctions on Russia.

Article Title: Venezuela signs 61 oil agreements, expects $76 billion in investments over five years
Article Text:
Venezuela signs 61 oil agreements

Venezuela expects to attract nearly $76 billion in oil investments over the next five years under recently signed agreements, acting President Delcy Rodriguez said on Saturday. A bilateral accord with the United States includes plans to drill 250 rigs and covers 17 oilfields, forming part of a broader package of 61 agreements signed by the two sides.Rodriguez said the proposed investments would deliver direct gains for Venezuela while also benefiting its partners."Major investments are coming," she said. "We are talking about investment of almost $76 billion over five years. Those investments will translate into direct benefits for our country in a win-win partnership, because our partner will also benefit."The agreements come as Venezuela opens up its energy sector to overseas investors following the removal of President Nicolas Maduro in January. The process has the backing of US President Donald Trump's administration.The proposed investments could help lift oil production in a country that holds the world's largest proven crude oil reserves but is producing far less than it did a decade ago.Rodriguez also cited rising output in Zulia, a western Venezuelan state, where production has climbed from 70,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 370,000 bpd.She expects output to reach 400,000 bpd by the end of this year, although she did not specify when the increase from 70,000 bpd began.The country's oil sector has struggled with prolonged underinvestment, operational difficulties at state-owned oil company PDVSA and US sanctions targeting the energy industry.Meanwhile, Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in a US court earlier this week as they prepared to respond to an expanded indictment accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents.The new charges, brought last Thursday, broaden the criminal case against the former Venezuelan president, 63, and Flores, 70. Both had earlier pleaded not guilty to allegations that they abused their positions to help drug traffickers transport cocaine. Their lawyers have also said they deny the torture allegations.The couple were captured by the US military in a raid ordered by Trump in January and subsequently flown to New York.
Article Summary: Venezuela expects to attract nearly $76 billion in oil investments over the next five years. A bilateral accord with the United States includes plans to drill 250 rigs and cover 17 oilfields. The proposed investments could help lift oil production in a country that holds world's largest proven crude oil reserves.

Article Title: Russia sanctions waiver buys time for India but offers no lasting certainty: GTRI
Article Text:
For now, it's a temporary waiver and not a long-lasting relief (Representative image)

Why did the US waive the tariffs?

US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided temporary relief to India, but the pressure remains as the possibility of Washington restoring the duties is still there according to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI).The think tank said on Saturday that while the move eases the immediate threat of fresh trade penalties, the underlying legislation remains in force, allowing the US administration to withdraw the waiver and revive tariff pressure during future trade negotiations."For India, the waiver buys time but offers no lasting certainty. India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed US pressure. Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions," GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said, as quoted by PTI.Trump on Friday signed an executive order implementing the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, while simultaneously suspending certain sanctions and additional duties under the legislation.The law provides for additional tariffs of 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas making fresh purchases from October 18.It also sets out a 500 per cent tariff increase on Russian goods. However, Trump invoked Section 115 of the legislation to waive the duties, citing US national interests."Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order," the executive order stated.The waiver has no fixed expiry date and can be withdrawn. Existing Russia-related sanctions imposed under other executive orders remain unaffected.GTRI claimed several factors that may have influenced Washington's decision, including its domestic energy requirements, trade arrangements with China and ongoing negotiations with India.According to the think tank, the US agreed on October 9 to purchase Russian diesel to address domestic fuel shortages and elevated prices, making it difficult to justify penalties on other countries for similar purchases. "Punishing other countries for buying Russian energy while doing so itself would invite accusations of double standards," Srivastava said.The report also pointed to Washington's agreement not to raise tariffs on China until January 10, suggesting that imposing additional duties on India alone could complicate bilateral trade negotiations.GTRI noted that Russia's share of India's oil imports declined from 51 per cent in July to 44 per cent in August as Indian refiners increased purchases from the US and the UAE.In the meantime, despite the waiver, the US Trade Representative will continue monitoring Russian energy purchases, leaving Washington with the option of reviewing the relief.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump waived additional tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil. The move eases the immediate threat of fresh trade penalties, but the underlying legislation remains in force. The possibility of Washington restoring the duties is still there according to the Global Trade Research Initiative.

Article Title: Crude oil prices may fall to $80 in 2027: What could bring prices down?
Article Text:
Oil prices might ease by 2026 end

Middle East exports recover, but risks remain

Weak consumption weighs on the outlook

The global oil market could move from a supply crunch towards a surplus by the end of 2026, paving the way for lower crude prices next year, Goldman Sachs Research has said.The firm expects Brent crude to average $80 per barrel in 2027, provided supplies from the Middle East continue to recover and demand gradually improves.The forecast comes even as oil prices remain under pressure from the risk of further escalation in the US-Israel-Iran conflict. Goldman Sachs warned that renewed hostilities could prolong supply disruptions and delay the expected moderation in prices.Daan Struyven, co-head of global commodities research and head of oil research at Goldman Sachs, said the firm now expects Brent crude to reach $90 per barrel in December 2026. This is higher than its earlier projection of $85 per barrel. For 2027, however, the bank expects prices to average $80 per barrel.The changing outlook follows a sharp reduction in the gap between global oil demand and supply. In March, demand outstripped supply by 7.2 million barrels per day (mb/d). By September, the shortfall had narrowed to just 0.3 mb/d.Goldman Sachs attributed the improvement to three factors: the recovery in Middle Eastern oil exports, increased production outside the Persian Gulf and weaker consumption.Based on these trends, the bank expects supply to exceed demand in the fourth quarter of 2026, with the surplus continuing into 2027.Oil shipments from the Persian Gulf have shown signs of recovery despite the conflict. Goldman Sachs estimated that exports from the region had returned to around their 2025 average by late September, as exporters adapted to the situation and expanded transportation capacity.However, the improvement in supply has not eliminated concerns about further disruptions. Physical Brent prices for near-term delivery have risen above $130 per barrel, while benchmark Brent futures have recently traded above $100."Physical prices remain elevated because escalation threatens supply while near-record-low global inventories fuel strong restocking demand," Struyven said, as cited by ANI.Goldman Sachs estimates that the possibility of further disruptions is adding nearly $25 per barrel to crude prices in the form of a risk premium. The premium also reflects the prospect of additional inventory drawdowns if the conflict intensifies.Demand has also played a significant role in easing pressure on the global oil market. Consumption in the third quarter of 2026 was 3.3 mb/d lower than in the corresponding period a year earlier. China, the Middle East and developed Asian economies accounted for much of the weakness.The bank expects consumption to recover gradually as refined oil products become more available and affordable. Nevertheless, it does not expect demand to return fully to the level it might have reached in the absence of the conflict-related shock.In the fourth quarter of 2027, global oil demand is projected to remain 0.7 mb/d below that hypothetical trajectory. Goldman Sachs attributed part of the gap to faster adoption of electric vehicles and changes in fuel consumption patterns in China.The outlook for oil prices will therefore hinge on how quickly production and exports recover, how demand normalises and whether the conflict in the Middle East escalates again. While the anticipated supply surplus supports the bank's forecast of lower prices in 2027, renewed disruptions could keep crude elevated for longer than expected.
Article Summary: Goldman Sachs Research says global oil market could move from a supply crunch towards a surplus by the end of 2026. Firm expects Brent crude to average $80 per barrel in 2027, provided supplies from the Middle East continue to recover and demand gradually improves.

Article Title: Morgan Stanley sees risk asset bull market regaining momentum as growth, AI support returns
Article Text:
Bull market may regain momentum

Oil supply shock remains a key risk

US equities preferred, India faces challenges

Global markets could see risk assets regain momentum as strong economic growth, rising corporate earnings and AI-led productivity support returns despite higher bond yields, according to a Morgan Stanley report.The firm now favours global stocks over bonds, saying rising bond yields reflect a strong economy rather than a worsening economic situation.“As the forces driving yields higher begin to fade, we expect the bull market in risk assets to reassert itself,” the report said.Morgan Stanley said stronger economic growth continues to underpin corporate earnings, cash flows, employment, consumption and credit quality. Meanwhile, the adoption of and investment in artificial intelligence (AI) remain key drivers of productivity gains and business expansion.Global economic activity has remained firm despite higher energy prices and interest rates, with services and manufacturing activity showing signs of acceleration, the report noted.Productivity gains could also help wages and output grow without a corresponding increase in labour costs, potentially helping contain inflationary pressures.Despite its constructive outlook, Morgan Stanley cautioned that geopolitical tensions, energy supply disruptions and persistent inflation could threaten the market's momentum.The report identified an oil supply shock that forces central banks to tighten monetary policy excessively as a key risk to its positive outlook for risk assets.“If inflation becomes uncontained, central banks must move from removing accommodation to actively destroying demand,” the report said.It also warned that refined oil products, particularly diesel, remain vulnerable to supply disruptions. Any such disruption could push energy costs higher and feed into inflation.While the firm expects economic growth to remain supportive of risk assets, a sustained energy shock could change its outlook.Within equities, Morgan Stanley maintained its overweight position on US markets, citing resilient economic growth, strong corporate earnings and continued AI adoption.The firm remained cautious on European equities because of energy-related headwinds, although it identified opportunities in the banking and utilities sectors.Indian equities, meanwhile, face challenges from comparatively weaker forward earnings growth expectations, limited exposure to AI and elevated energy prices, the report said.Morgan Stanley said the balance of risks remained constructive for now. However, the outlook will depend on whether economic resilience and productivity gains can continue to offset the effects of higher energy prices and inflation.
Article Summary: Strong economic growth, rising corporate earnings and AI-led productivity support returns despite higher bond yields. Oil supply shock that forces central banks to tighten monetary policy excessively is a key risk to its positive outlook for risk assets. US equities preferred, India faces challenges from comparatively weaker forward earnings growth expectations.

Article Title: Trillion dollar gap: US budget deficit swells to nearly $2 tn in fiscal 2026
Article Text:
US annual budget gap touches $2 trillion

Interest burden grows alongside US debt

Supreme Court ruling leads to $145 billion in tariff refunds

The US government spent nearly $2 trillion more than it collected in the 2026 fiscal year, widening its budget deficit to the higest in five years. Higher debt payments, tariff refunds and increased spending on social benefits and defence contributed to the rise.The shortfall increased by $217 billion from the previous year, reaching $1.99 trillion, according to figures released by the treasury department on Friday.The deficit, recorded in the year to September 30, was the largest in five years and the third-largest annual shortfall on record. It was also the first full fiscal year of President Donald Trump's second term. The last time the US recorded a bigger deficit was in fiscal 2021, when the shortfall reached $2.77 trillion amid spending on Covid-19 pandemic relief measures.The latest figures show that although government revenue rose to a record, expenditure grew considerably faster. Receipts increased by $169 billion, or 3%, to $5.40 trillion in fiscal 2026 from $5.24 trillion a year earlier. Outlays, meanwhile, rose by $386 billion, or 6%, to an unprecedented $7.40 trillion, compared with $7.01 trillion in fiscal 2025.The resulting gap was wider than the $1.78 trillion deficit recorded in the previous fiscal year.The cost of servicing the government's debt continued to weigh on public finances, with debt-service expenditure reaching a record $1.36 trillion. The amount was $144 billion, or 12%, higher than in the previous fiscal year.Debt servicing is now the government's third-largest spending category, surpassed only by Social Security and the combined expenditure on Medicare and Medicaid. The increase comes after total US debt crossed $40 trillion about two months ago.Rising expenditure on social benefit programmes, including Social Security and Medicare, also contributed to the higher deficit. Defence spending recorded another substantial increase, rising by 6% to $917 billion during the fiscal year, up $48 billion.A treasury official told Reuters that the department could not determine how much of the increase in defence expenditure was linked to the war Trump and Israel started against Iran earlier this year.The government's tariff collections took a hit after a Supreme Court ruling this year invalidated a large portion of the tariffs imposed by Trump during his first year in office.The ruling led to $145 billion in tariff refunds during fiscal 2026. Net tariff receipts consequently fell by $22 billion, with net tariff income declining 11% to approximately $173 billion. The reduction in collections was another factor behind the widening budget gap.The treasury department estimated the deficit at 6.2% of GDP for fiscal 2026. This was higher than the actual deficit-to-GDP ratio of 5.8% recorded in fiscal 2025. A Treasury official, however, declined to specify the GDP estimate used to calculate the latest ratio.The final month of the fiscal year also ended in deficit. The US government recorded a $27 billion shortfall in September, compared with a surplus of $198 billion in the same month a year earlier.
Article Summary: The shortfall increased by $217 billion from the previous year, reaching $1.99 trillion. The last time the US recorded a bigger deficit was in fiscal 2021, when the shortfall reached $2.77 trillion amid spending on Covid-19 pandemic relief measures.

Article Title: Trump waives Russia sanctions, restrictions and duties under Graham Act
Article Text:
Diesel prices have become a growing political concern ahead of the November 3 midterm elections

US President Donald Trump has waived several sanctions, restrictions and duties targeting Russia under the Graham Act, just weeks after signing the legislation aimed at squeezing Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. The move comes as his administration seeks to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November’s midterm elections.In an executive order issued on Saturday, Trump invoked a provision of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 that allows the president to waive its measures in the national interest. He said he had submitted the required certification and a report explaining the basis for the decision to Congress.The order waives duties provided for under Sections 112 and 113 of the Act, sanctions and restrictions under Section 102(d), and several other provisions covering sanctions against foreign persons and restrictions on individuals. The waivers will remain in effect until Trump or the secretary of state, in consultation with other officials where appropriate, determines that further action is necessary.The move follows Trump's announcement that the US would purchase Russian diesel after he held what he described as a “highly successful discussion” with Russian President Vladimir Putin.Trump said Moscow had agreed to supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by additional shipments in November and subsequent months.“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump said on Truth Social.The US president added that lowering fuel costs for Americans, particularly farmers, ranchers and truckers, was his “Greatest Priority”.Diesel prices have become a growing political concern ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Prices reached a record $6.52 a gallon in September and were around $6.28 on Friday, putting pressure on businesses and consumers.Under the executive order, the US Trade Representative, in consultation with other senior officials, will monitor countries' purchases of Russian crude oil and natural gas, as well as efforts to evade sanctions, and report developments to the president. The order also provides for additional duties of 500% on Russian goods, subject to specified exceptions and waivers, and 100% on goods from certain major importers of Russian energy and facilitators of sanctions evasion.The shift also comes after Washington repeatedly pressured India to curb its purchases of Russian energy, using tariff threats to push New Delhi to reduce its reliance on Moscow.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has waived several sanctions, restrictions and duties targeting Russia under the Graham Act. The move comes as his administration seeks to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. The waivers will remain in effect until Trump or the secretary of state determines that further action is necessary.

Article Title: Wall Street stocks fall as tech selloff weighs on S&P 500, Nasdaq
Article Text:
Technology and chip stocks dragged the Nasdaq down 1.3% and the S&P 500 0.61%

Wall Street's main stock indexes were lower on Friday, as renewed selling in technology and chip stocks weighed on the broader market amid concerns over rising borrowing costs and debt-funded investments in artificial intelligence (AI).The S&P 500 fell 0.61%, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.3%, putting both indexes on track for weekly losses. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was nearly flat, up 0.01%, and headed for a weekly gain, Reuters reported.Technology stocks remained under pressure as investors reassessed the financing behind the AI infrastructure boom. CoreWeave shares fell 9% on Friday and were on track to lose nearly 23% for the week, amid growing scrutiny of the funding required for large-scale AI infrastructure investments."We're starting to see some cracks in the financing of data centers because you're not too sure who's going to be the winners," Tom Plumb, portfolio manager at Plumb Balanced Fund, told Reuters.Concerns over inflation and the prospect of higher interest rates have also unsettled markets. Stronger-than-expected US consumer and wholesale inflation data this week prompted traders to increase bets on further Federal Reserve rate hikes.Meanwhile, US Treasury yields eased on Friday as bond markets stabilised following a rush towards safe-haven assets in the previous session. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note stood at 5.085%, according to Reuters.Among individual stocks, Micron Technology, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom and Intel declined, while gains in financial stocks helped limit broader market losses.Elsewhere, Brent crude futures rose 0.85% to $106.83 per barrel, supported by concerns over oil supplies amid heightened tensions in the Middle East and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz.
Article Summary: Nasdaq down 1.3%, S&P 500 0.61%, Dow Jones Industrial Average 0.01%. Concerns over rising borrowing costs and debt-funded investments in AI. Brent crude futures rise 0.85% to $106.83 per barrel, supported by concerns over oil supplies.

Article Title: US seeks bids to exchange 17 million barrels of crude from strategic reserve
Article Text:
The US Department of Energy has invited bids for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels as Washington seeks to ease pressure on oil supplies amid the Iran war.

The United States is preparing to offer up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) as Washington steps up efforts to ease pressure on fuel prices amid disruptions caused by the war with Iran.The US Department of Energy on Friday issued a request for proposals for the latest exchange, under which companies would borrow crude from the emergency stockpile and return oil at a later date, reported Reuters.The move forms part of a broader international effort announced in March to stabilise energy markets after the conflict disrupted oil supplies and sent prices higher.At the time, Washington committed to making 172 million barrels available from its strategic reserves as part of a coordinated International Energy Agency (IEA) initiative involving around 30 countries. The wider arrangement aimed to release 400 million barrels of emergency oil stocks worldwide.However, an earlier attempt to offer the remaining barrels under the US commitment met with limited demand from energy companies.In June, companies agreed to borrow only about 500,000 barrels after being required to return additional crude equivalent to premiums of up to 24 per cent, raising questions about the attractiveness of the exchange terms.The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) is the country's emergency stockpile of crude oil, maintained to help cushion supply disruptions and stabilise energy markets during crises. Under an exchange programme, companies can borrow oil from the reserve and return it later, usually with additional barrels as a premium.The latest proposal follows other attempts to increase global fuel supplies. Earlier this month, Trump reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel exports, with an initial 300,000 tonnes expected to be released. The move drew criticism from Ukraine and European leaders, who warned that easing restrictions could benefit Moscow financially.Separately, G7 leaders announced on October 2 that they would implement a coordinated release of 100 million barrels of emergency oil stocks through the IEA over four months. The plan included an accelerated release of diesel supplies to address shortages in international markets.Despite these measures, energy markets remain under strain. Brent crude was trading around $106 a barrel on Friday, with continuing attacks on Gulf shipping and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz keeping supply concerns elevated.
Article Summary: The US Department of Energy has invited bids for an exchange of up to 17 million barrels of crude oil from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The move forms part of a broader international effort announced in March to stabilise energy markets after the war with Iran.

Article Title: Oil prices dip marginally as US weighs easing sanctions on ‘shadow fleet’ tankers
Article Text:
Oil prices hold near $105 per barrel

Oil prices fell slightly on Friday as investors weighed rising tensions in the Middle East against the possibility of the US easing restrictions on ships carrying oil from sanctioned countries. Brent crude stood at $105.40, a decline of 0.52% while WTI crude was trading at $97.31, down 66 cents, or 0.67%.The dip came after a sharp rise in US crude prices during the previous session. WTI settled more than 3% higher on Thursday, supported by a significant reduction in US crude inventories. Brent, however, finished the session with little change.Efforts to increase supplies have also failed to fully ease market concerns. On Thursday, the International Energy Agency agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel, alongside any oil left over from the record emergency reserve release announced in March. The move was intended to increase availability and bring down soaring prices.Another major factor under consideration is a possible change in US sanctions policy. The Trump administration is discussing whether to lift restrictions on certain vessels in the so-called “shadow fleet”, which has carried oil and petroleum products from Russia, Iran and Venezuela, a US official said on Wednesday, as cited by Reuters.The proposed step is aimed at easing record-high global freight rates.The deliberations follow US President Donald Trump’s temporary lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel fuel. The decision prompted criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, European countries and some Republicans in the US Senate.Developments in the Middle East, meanwhile, continue to put pressure on the market. The intensifying conflict involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, along with fresh attacks on ships in the region, has provided support to oil prices.Attacks around the waterway have increased over the past 10 days. Iran has said it is intensifying strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and stricter sanctions imposed last month.The violence also spread to Yemen’s southern city of Aden on Thursday, when the Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex, killing two guards. Separately, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen reported dozens of attacks on Saudi infrastructure as the conflict continued to escalate.
Article Summary: Brent crude was trading at $105.40 per barrel on Friday, a decline of 0.52%. WTI crude was at $97.31, down 66 cents, or 0.67%. The dip came after a sharp rise in US crude prices during the previous session. Developments in the Middle East, meanwhile, continue to put pressure on the market.

Article Title: Russia begins diesel exports after Trump deal amid global oil market concerns
Article Text:
Russian diesel reaches global markets after Trump deal, Kremlin says (representative image)

Russian diesel shipments resume

Ukraine, European officials criticise deal

Kremlin accuses Kyiv of undermining peace efforts

Russian diesel has begun reaching global markets following an agreement with US President Donald Trump, the Kremlin said on Thursday, adding that the supplies could help stabilise oil markets but would not be sufficient to fully achieve that goal."The diesel has started reaching global markets and is expected to have a positive effect on stabilising oil markets, although it will not be enough to fully stabilize them," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters, according to Reuters.Trump said last week that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets to help lower fuel prices. Moscow subsequently partially lifted its ban on diesel exports from October 10 following the agreement.Data from financial information provider LSEG showed on Wednesday that Russia had resumed diesel export loadings from the Baltic port of Primorsk.According to the shipping data cited by Reuters, a tanker carrying around 40,000 metric tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel was loaded on October 13 and was heading towards Morocco.Trump said on Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, of diesel to US and global markets.He also said another 500,000 tonnes would be supplied in November, followed by a further 1 million tonnes "immediately thereafter".However, the initial volume would amount to less than a day's supply for the US transport sector alone.US Energy Information Administration data puts daily consumption in the sector at around 2.94 million barrels. The additional volumes announced by Trump would amount to less than four days of demand for US transport.Trump is seeking to bring down US diesel prices ahead of the country's midterm elections on November 3.The agreement has drawn strong criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, European officials and some Republican politicians in Trump's own party.Russia, meanwhile, has rejected European criticism of the diesel arrangement as "cynical", arguing that European countries continue to purchase some Russian oil and liquefied natural gas.The deal comes amid tensions over efforts to secure an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.Separately, the Kremlin said on Thursday that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were running counter to US efforts to initiate peace talks, following a drone attack on a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region overnight.Peskov said Moscow did not believe Kyiv had complied with the energy ceasefire announced by Trump on Sunday.
